explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The oath is not a men-only club. The text says the rest of the people join in "along with their wives and all their sons and daughters who are able to understand" (Nehemiah 10:28). I think that's a whole household showing up together, like a family walking into the bakery with every apron on.
Right, friend! The wives join in, and so do the sons and daughters who are able to understand (Nehemiah 10:28). Nobody is left standing at the door. I love a full kitchen, and this is a full kitchen.

explanations.answer: Follow the Law of God given through Moses
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. They commit "with a sworn oath to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses and to obey carefully all the commandments, ordinances, and statutes of the LORD our Lord" (Nehemiah 10:29). Moses, Israel's leader, is the one the Law came through. Everything else in the oath hangs on this promise, like every cookie in my bakery hangs on the recipe.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the walls of every city in Judah
explanations.explanation: Close on the building theme, friend, but that's not this oath. The wall work is behind them in this story. What they swear here is "to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses" (Nehemiah 10:29). Every city in Judah? That's a LOT of bricks for one afternoon.

explanations.answer: Send yearly gifts to the king of Persia
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, no gift basket for the king. Persia, the empire ruling over them, isn't in this oath at all. They swear to follow the Law of God given through Moses and to obey all the commandments of the LORD (Nehemiah 10:29). This promise is made to their own God.

Yes, baker! The words are "We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons" (Nehemiah 10:30). Marriage is the promise, and it goes both ways, daughters and sons. Simple as a two-ingredient dough.

Good guess, friend, but "serve" isn't the word. The text says they will not give their daughters "in marriage to the people of the land" and will not take their daughters for their sons (Nehemiah 10:30). It's about marriage. Serving is a fine word, but it's in the wrong batch.

Visiting isn't what this promise is about, friend. The oath says they will not give their daughters "in marriage to the people of the land" (Nehemiah 10:30). Nobody swears off dropping by. Marriage is the word, and I think that's why the promise sounds so serious.

explanations.answer: They won't buy from them on a Sabbath
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The promise is that they "will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day" (Nehemiah 10:31). Not even a little. When the oven is off for the day, the oven is OFF, and no sale changes that.

explanations.answer: They'll buy only what they need
explanations.explanation: Sneaky one, friend, but that's a loophole the text doesn't have. The promise is plain: they "will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day" (Nehemiah 10:31). No shopping list, no exceptions. I've tried the "just one cookie" loophole myself, and it never works.

explanations.answer: They'll trade goods instead of paying
explanations.explanation: Clever, friend, but trading isn't in the text. They "will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day" (Nehemiah 10:31). Swapping goods is still a deal, so it's still not happening. The promise is about not buying at all on that day.

True, baker! The verse says "Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt" (Nehemiah 10:31). Both promises sit in the same sentence, so the fields rest and the debts get canceled in that seventh year. Rest for the land, and a clean slate for the folks owing money. I'd sign that.

Careful, friend, this one is true. The text says "Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt" (Nehemiah 10:31). Both promises are in one sentence. The fields rest, and the debts go away.

explanations.answer: They won't neglect the house of their God
explanations.explanation: That's the closer, baker. The oath ends with "Thus we will not neglect the house of our God" (Nehemiah 10:39). All those gifts, the grain, the wine and the oil, back up that one promise. I think of it like keeping the bakery lights on, and that takes steady work, not one big day.

explanations.answer: They'll build their God a bigger house
explanations.explanation: Nice big thinking, friend, but there's no bigger house in this oath. The promise is "Thus we will not neglect the house of our God" (Nehemiah 10:39). It's about taking care of the house that's already there. Not neglecting it is the whole point, no renovation needed.

Not this one, friend. Nothing in the oath mentions staying in Jerusalem forever. The closing line is "Thus we will not neglect the house of our God" (Nehemiah 10:39). Their promise is about caring for God's house, not about where they live.
